deep.reconstruction:
OVERVIEW. The page continues the previous folio. Gauss works through primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) between 2089 and 2357, and also some primes above 2357. For each p he lists the cycles of reduced binary quadratic forms of determinant +p, in Gauss's convention (a,b,c) with b^2 - ac = p. He also tabulates, for primes whose positive determinant p has more than one class, two numbers: the class number for determinant +p, and the class number for determinant -p.

A. CYCLE COMPUTATIONS (lower two-thirds of the page)

(i) First line: the principal cycle. The first line after each prime is the principal cycle, which is the same as the sequence of denominators Q_k in the continued fraction expansion of sqrt(p). Write a0 = floor(sqrt(p)). The recursion is m_0 = 0, Q_0 = 1, then
- a_k = floor((a0 + m_k)/Q_k),
- m_{k+1} = a_k Q_k - m_k,
- Q_{k+1} = (p - m_{k+1}^2)/Q_k.
Equivalently, each neighbour form (Q_k, m_{k+1}, -Q_{k+1}) satisfies m^2 + Q_k Q_{k+1} = p.

Worked example, p = 2357 (my steps; a0 = 48):
- Q_1 = 53 (m = 48)
- Q_2 = 44 (m = 5)
- Q_3 = 19 (m = 39)
- Q_4 = 52 (m = 37)
- Q_5 = 41 (m = 15)
- Q_6 = 41 (m = 26)
This matches the manuscript '1.53.44.19.52.41.41 &c.'

Gauss stops at the first repeated value Q_k = Q_{k+1} (the midpoint of the odd period). At that point p = m_{k+1}^2 + Q_k^2. That is the classical continued-fraction (Legendre–Gauss) construction of p as a sum of two squares. The squares themselves are not written; they are implied (my addition):
- 2357 = 26^2 + 41^2
- 2341 = 46^2 + 15^2
- 2333 = 22^2 + 43^2
- 2309 = 10^2 + 47^2 (full recursion checked: 5, 20, 61, 25, 4, 71, 23, 20, 47, 47)
- 2297 = 44^2 + 19^2
- 2293 = 42^2 + 23^2
- 2281 = 16^2 + 45^2
- 2273 = 8^2 + 47^2
- 2269 = 30^2 + 37^2
- 2237 = 46^2 + 11^2
- 2221 = 14^2 + 45^2
- 2213 = 2^2 + 47^2
- 2161 = 44^2 + 15^2
- 2153 = 28^2 + 37^2
- 2141 = 46^2 + 5^2
- 2137 = 36^2 + 29^2
- 2129 = 40^2 + 23^2
- 2113 = 32^2 + 33^2
- 2089 = 8^2 + 45^2

(ii) Lines beginning with 4. For p ≡ 5 (mod 8) whose principal cycle does not contain 4, Gauss computes a further cycle starting with 4. This happens for 2357, 2341, 2269 and 2221; these lines are marked '0.3'. By contrast, 4 occurs in the principal cycles of 2333, 2309, 2293 and 2237, and those primes get no second line.

Example, p = 2357, starting from the form (4, 47, -37), since 47^2 + 4·37 = 2357. Applying the same neighbour rule gives the successive outer coefficients 37, 44, 47, 31, 43, 52, 13, 76, 11, 83 and then 4 again. The cycle closes, and it matches the manuscript '4.37.44.47.31.43.52.13.76.11.83.4'.

Interpretation (mine): the form with leading coefficient 4 lies outside the principal class. This is the case where forms of determinant p have three times as many classes as the improperly primitive forms (Disquisitiones art. 256, the h(4p) = 3h(p) phenomenon). The '0.3' marker plausibly records this.

(iii) Further lines starting with 7, 49, 3, 15, etc. These are cycles of non-principal classes for primes with class number above 1:
- 2213: (7, 43, -52)
- 2153: lines starting with 7 and with 49
- 2089: lines starting with 3 and with 15
This is consistent with the class numbers in the top table (2213: 3; 2153: 5; 2089: 3).

B. TOP TABLE. Entries have the form 'p . h+ . h-'. The middle number is the number of classes for determinant +p: 3, 5, 7, 9 or 11. Examples:
- 1297: 11
- 2917 and 1129: 9
- 2029, 1601, 1009: 7
The third number is the number of classes for determinant -p, i.e. the modern h(-4p).

This reading is confirmed by the next page. There primes are filed under exactly these numbers, e.g. 2357 under 42, 2269 and 2341 under 30, 2221 under 18. The next page's small cases fit the modern h(-4p):
- h(-20) = h(-52) = h(-148) = 2
- h(-68) = 4
- h(-116) = 6
- h(-164) = 8
The parities also fit: h(-4p) ≡ 2 (mod 4) for p ≡ 5 (mod 8), and ≡ 0 (mod 4) for p ≡ 1 (mod 8).

C. AVERAGES (top centre)
- 33, 29, 23 → mean 28 1/3
- 40, 36, 24 → mean 33 1/3
- mean of those two means = 30 5/6
- 29 and 33 → 31; 23 and 40 → 31 1/2; together 31 1/4

The list '12.370, 13.412, 14.444, 15.488, 16.548, 17.586' looks like running totals (count n, sum). Note 370/12 = 30 5/6, the same average. The increments 42, 32, 44, 60, 38 equal the h(-4p) values of 2357, 2153, 2089, 2081, 2069. So Gauss appears to be studying the mean of h(-4p) over primes whose positive determinant has a nontrivial class group. That is an empirical class-number-statistics inquiry.

The right-hand column '4 49, 8 51, 9 52, 12 54, 14 59, 19 60, 25 61, 29 63, 41, 42' is unclear; possibly a distribution or rank count. It is not reconstructed with certainty.
errors: No arithmetic errors found in the cycles checked in full: 2357 (principal cycle and 4-cycle), 2309, and the start of the 2213 7-cycle.
Every terminal symmetric pair checked gives p = m^2 + Q^2 exactly.
The meaning of '0.3', of the six averaged numbers (33, 29, 23, 40, 36, 24) and of the right-hand column cannot be established with certainty from this page alone.

results.what: Principal cycles of reduced forms of determinant p (continued-fraction denominators of sqrt p), stopped at the symmetric point to obtain p = x^2 + y^2, for primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 from 2089 to 2357.
results.modern_name: Continued fraction / cycle-of-reduced-forms algorithm for representing a prime as a sum of two squares (Legendre's method)
results.usually_credited_to: Legendre (1798); also Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), arts. 183–187

results.what: For p ≡ 5 mod 8, testing whether a form with leading coefficient 4 lies in the principal cycle; if not, computing its separate cycle (class number of determinant p is three times that of the improperly primitive forms).
results.modern_name: h(4p) = 3h(p) versus h(4p) = h(p), i.e. whether the fundamental unit of Q(sqrt p) has half-integral coordinates
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones art. 256 (relation between properly and improperly primitive classes); Eisenstein/Dirichlet later

results.what: Table of primes with class number of determinant +p greater than 1 (3, 5, 7, 9, 11), paired with the number of classes of determinant -p.
results.modern_name: Tables of class numbers of real and imaginary quadratic orders h(4p), h(-4p)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (class number tables, partly published in Werke II)

results.what: Averaging h(-4p) over selected primes (running totals 370/12 = 30 5/6, etc.).
results.modern_name: Empirical average order of class numbers (cf. Gauss's conjectured mean value of class numbers, Disq. art. 302)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (average class number statements, Disq. art. 302); proved by Lipschitz/Mertens/Siegel

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine but laborious class-number and cycle computations of exactly the kind Gauss is known to have made for his tables (Disquisitiones arts. 187, 256, 302–304; Werke II tables). The comparison of h(-4p) for primes with nontrivial positive-determinant class number is a minor but characteristic empirical detail. Nothing here would be credited to someone later.
